summary: Supply the short-answer question 1, the short-answer question 2, the short-answer question 3 and the document-based question and the AP® World calculator solves for composite score (0-130). It suits whatever you happen to be working on. Change one value and the results step aside until you press Calculate again, which is what makes it easy to see how much the answer really depends on that one input.

sections.title: How does the AP® World calculator work?
sections.html:
The AP® World calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports composite score (0-130) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the short-answer question 1 (0-3), the short-answer question 2 (0-3), the short-answer question 3 (0-3) and the document-based question (0-7).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Multiple-choice (0-55) = 10, Short-answer question 1 (0-3) = 10, Short-answer question 2 (0-3) = 10 and Short-answer question 3 (0-3) = 10. The calculator returns Composite score (0-130) = 175 and AP® score (1-5) = 5.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Composite score (0-130) = 175 and AP® score (1-5) = 5 should be roughly the size you expected from Multiple-choice (0-55) = 10 and Short-answer question 1 (0-3) = 10.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The AP® World calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the short-answer question 1, the short-answer question 2 and the short-answer question 3 — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

faq.q: What does the AP® World calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns composite score (0-130), derived from the short-answer question 1, the short-answer question 2 and the short-answer question 3. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the AP® World calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the short-answer question 1, the short-answer question 2, the short-answer question 3 and the document-based question, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Composite score (0-130) = 175. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the AP® World calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
